name: Ebstein anomaly
aliases: Ebstein malformation of the tricuspid valve

reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC guidelines
clinicalPearls: A congenital malformation in which the tricuspid valve leaflets are displaced apically into the right ventricle, so part of the ventricle is incorporated into the right atrium
The displacement creates an atrialised portion of right ventricle, a small functional right ventricle, and usually significant tricuspid regurgitation
Presentation ranges widely, from severe cyanotic disease in the newborn to incidental diagnosis in an adult with mild disease
An associated atrial septal defect or patent foramen ovale can allow right-to-left shunting and cyanosis or paradoxical embolism
There is a strong association with accessory pathways and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, so supraventricular tachyarrhythmias are common
Echocardiography is diagnostic, demonstrating leaflet displacement and quantifying tricuspid regurgitation and right heart size
Management depends on severity and includes arrhythmia treatment, and surgical valve repair or replacement in symptomatic or deteriorating patients
It has historically been linked to fetal lithium exposure, though the absolute risk is low
reference.pathophysiology: In Ebstein anomaly, failure of normal delamination of the tricuspid valve during development displaces the septal and posterior leaflets downward into the right ventricle. This divides the right ventricle into a thin, poorly contractile atrialised segment continuous with the right atrium and a reduced functional chamber. The malformed, often tethered valve leaks, producing tricuspid regurgitation and progressive right atrial dilatation. Where an interatrial communication exists, elevated right atrial pressure can drive right-to-left shunting and cyanosis. Associated accessory conduction pathways predispose to re-entrant tachyarrhythmias.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of neonatal cyanosis such as tetralogy of Fallot or pulmonary atresia
Tricuspid valve dysplasia without apical displacement
Right heart dilatation from an isolated atrial septal defect
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography to define leaflet displacement, tricuspid regurgitation, and right heart function
12-lead ECG for pre-excitation and atrial arrhythmias
Cardiac MRI for right ventricular volumes and function
Assessment for an interatrial shunt and its direction
Exercise or oximetry testing to detect exertional desaturation
redFlags: Severe neonatal cyanosis or heart failure
Rapid supraventricular tachycardia, especially with an accessory pathway
Progressive right heart failure or worsening cyanosis
Paradoxical embolism or stroke through an interatrial shunt
reference.prognosis: Prognosis correlates with the degree of leaflet displacement, right ventricular function, and severity of tricuspid regurgitation. Mildly affected adults may live for decades with few symptoms, whereas severe neonatal presentations carry high mortality; arrhythmias and progressive right heart failure are important determinants of long-term outcome, and surgical repair can improve symptoms in selected patients.
pitfalls: Underestimating arrhythmic risk from an associated accessory pathway
Overlooking a right-to-left shunt as a cause of cyanosis or paradoxical embolism
Attributing right heart dilatation solely to an atrial septal defect
Delaying surgical referral until right ventricular function is severely impaired
Failing to counsel about pregnancy and hereditary considerations
